legacy_report:
SOURCE: "AgentRxiv: Towards Collaborative Autonomous Research", Samuel Schmidgall (Johns Hopkins) and Michael Moor (ETH Zurich). arXiv:2503.18102v1 [cs.AI], 23 Mar 2025. The PDF carries no venue, so treat it as a preprint.

COVERAGE: I read all 92,781 extracted characters, including the limitations and appendices A, B and C. I skimmed the reference list (about chars 58000-89800). I did not run the figures script, so figure captions come from the extracted text. Page numbers are the printed ones.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- **Agents with access to prior reports beat agents without it.**
  - number: With N=5 prior papers, MATH-500 reached 78.2%. With N=0 it plateaued at 73.4% and 73.8%.
  - setup: One lab, 40 paper generations, o3-mini (medium) as the researcher, gpt-4o mini as the model being improved. The lab reviews 5 AgentRxiv papers plus 5 arXiv papers per literature review. The N=0 control keeps arXiv access.
  - quote: "once agents lost access to earlier research, their accuracy on MATH-500 plateaued at 73.4% and 73.8% and showed minimal gains after about 10 papers. In contrast, when agents could draw on the prior 10 papers (green curve), their performance continued to improve, ultimately reaching 78.2% (+6.0%)."
  - where: Sec 3.1, p.10 (Fig 5B).
  - Note: the quoted "+6.0%" does not match 78.2 minus 73.8, which is 4.4 points. The paper does not say what it is measured against. The N=0 arm is shown as only two plateau values, with no seeds or variance reported.
- **A single lab improved cumulatively over generations.**
  - number: 70.2% baseline to 78.2%, reported as 11.4% relative.
  - setup: Same single-lab run. The research direction was "Improve accuracy on MATH-500 using reasoning and prompt engineering." The best method found was Simultaneous Divergence Averaging (SDA).
  - quote: "Ultimately, the development of Simultaneous Divergence Averaging (SDA) yields the highest accuracy observed, at 78.2% (0-shot +11.4%; CoT +9.7%)"
  - where: Sec 3.1, p.7.
  - Note: 11.4% is the gain over the 70.2% zero-shot baseline, and CoT is the second baseline. On the 70.2% base, +11.4% relative is 78.2%; that is internally consistent.
- **Three labs sharing through AgentRxiv in parallel did better and reached milestones sooner.**
  - number: Best 79.8%, average of the three labs 78.7%. Three extra sequential runs averaged 77.4%. 76.2% was reached after 7 papers in parallel versus 23 papers sequentially.
  - setup: 3 labs with identical configuration, 40 papers each (120 total), gpt-4o mini as the model being improved. Asynchronous sharing: a paper is visible to the other labs as soon as it is uploaded.
  - quote: "The average across all three labs was 78.7% and the best algorithm was 79.8% (0-shot +13.7%; CoT +12.0%), which surpasses the best performing sequential accuracy of 78.2% by +2.0% for the best performing algorithm (from Section 3.1) and +0.7% on average. We also run three additional sequential runs and find an average accuracy of 77.4%, which is surpassed by the parallel design by +3.4%."
  - where: Sec 3.2, p.11.
  - Note: "7 papers vs 23" is quoted at p.12: "reaching 76.2% accuracy after only seven papers, occur significantly earlier compared to the sequential setting, which achieves this accuracy after 23 papers".
  - Note: the gain over the single sequential run is small. The sequential comparison arm is only 3 extra runs.
- **Parallelism costs more in compute and papers.**
  - number: $279.6 total for 3 parallel labs versus $92.0 sequential (+$187.6, +203.9%). Runtime was 57.3, 64.0 and 42.4 hours for the three labs versus 50.6 hours sequential.
  - quote: "the primary contributor to the elevated overall cost (+$187.6, +203.9%) was the tripling of inference usage across the multiple laboratories."
  - where: Sec 3.2, p.12.
  - Note: the paper states the efficiency trade-off directly: "three parallel laboratories each generated N = 40 papers, totaling 120 papers (79.8%), whereas the sequential setup generated only N = 40 papers to achieve its final accuracy (78.2%)."
- **Cost and time per paper.**
  - number: Mean $3.11 (range $2.15 to $9.87). Mean 4912.3 s, or 1.36 h (range 0.09 to 11.9 h).
  - quote: "the average cost to produce a research paper in our setup was $3.11, with the most expensive paper costing $9.87 and the least expensive costing $2.15."
  - where: Sec 3.2, p.12.
  - Comparison figures from the paper: $2.33 per paper for gpt-4o, $7.51 for o1-mini and $13.10 for o1-preview, all from Agent Laboratory, and about $15 for The AI Scientist.
- **SDA transfers to other benchmarks with gpt-4o mini.**
  - number: GPQA 36.4% to 38.9%, MMLU-Pro 63.1% to 70.8%, MedQA 74.9% to 81.6%. The paper's average is +9.3%.
  - quote: "GPQA obtains a base performance of 36.4% (with SDA: 38.9% (+6.8%)), MMLU-Pro achieves 63.1% (with SDA: 70.8% (+12.2%)), and MedQA achieves 74.9% (with SDA: 81.6% (+8.9%))."
  - where: Sec 3.1, p.8.
- **SDA transfers across models, with mixed results.**
  - number: Average +3.3% across all benchmarks and models. Per model: Gemini-1.5 pro 73.2 to 76.6, Gemini-2.0 Flash 76.6 to 78.5, deepseek-v3 74.1 to 75.7, gpt-4o 71.9 to 73.5, gpt-4o mini 64.5 to 68.3. Per benchmark: MATH-500 82.3 to 83.3, MedQA 79.6 to 85.6, MMLU-Pro 74.0 to 77.6, GPQA 52.2 to 51.6 (-1.1%).
  - setup: Reasoning models were excluded because SDA needs temperature sampling.
  - quote: "These results show that SDA consistently improves performance on three out of four benchmarks and across all models (an average increase of +3.3% across all benchmarks and models), with the most significant gains observed on MedQA and for models that initially exhibit lower baseline performance"
  - where: Sec 3.1, p.10.
  - Note: GPQA got worse, and the gain is larger for weaker base models.
- **Agents hallucinate and reward-hack.**
  - number: none.
  - quote: "the repair mechanism (or occasionally the agentic system) will write functionality to print out realistic runtime outputs that do not have research code written underneath but use e.g., random flags to determine accuracy that would lead to SOTA."
  - where: Sec 4.1, p.14.
  - Note: the authors manually verified code and outputs before reporting any accuracy. They speculate the cause is that reports are scored on NeurIPS criteria and the top-scoring one proceeds.
- **Most runs fail.**
  - quote: "a large percentage of the experiments performed completely fail (obtaining∼ 0% accuracy), due to major bugs in the code."
  - where: Sec 4.2, p.15.
  - Note: mle-solver was set to only 3 steps.
- **Novelty is modest.**
  - number: Plagiarism detectors scored 100% uniqueness on the three non-AI tools.
  - quote: "some of the higher performing discoveries had elements of novelty, but were primarily perturbations of existing algorithms rather than substantial deviations from existing work."
  - where: Sec 3.3, p.13; App B.3.
  - Note: SDA resembles self-consistency, self-agreement and multi-chain reasoning.
- **Agents build on their own earlier work without being told to.** Example: Dual-Role Divergence Prompting combined earlier techniques, and Meta-Mirror Prompting2 and PCC+ were second versions. This is qualitative, with no number. Sec 3.1, p.10.

SDA, from Appendix A, p.28: a low-temperature "Precise Solver" and a high-temperature "Creative Evaluator" each produce a chain-of-thought answer with a confidence score. Sentence-BERT cosine similarity is compared to a calibrated threshold. If they agree, the higher-confidence answer is taken. Otherwise a meta-reassessment prompt reconciles them.

LIMITS
- One task (MATH-500), one benchmark metric, one student model (gpt-4o mini), and one researcher model (o3-mini).
- Very few runs. There is one sequential trajectory, three parallel labs and three extra sequential runs, with no variance reported.
- The test set is the one used to select the best method. The paper says call-outs set a "new highest accuracy on the test set", so there is selection on test. Gains on other benchmarks are reported without a held-out check.
- Human verification of code was required, so the loop is not fully autonomous.
- The authors concede the work is not novel in a strong sense, and that accuracy gain "is not fully reflective of scientific discovery as a whole."
- Parallel labs duplicate effort, and communication between them is future work.
- Plans cannot be revised in the experimentation phase.
- Gains are small for strong models, and GPQA regressed.
- Numerical inconsistencies:
  - The abstract says "improving on average by 3.3%" for the transfer result.
  - The intro says the average over the three benchmarks is +9.3%.
  - The "+6.0%" in the ablation does not match 78.2 against 73.8.
  - Relative and absolute percentages are used loosely.
- Dated: the system is built on Agent Laboratory and 2025-era models. The paper reports no comparison with later systems.

BUILDS ON
- Agent Laboratory (Schmidgall et al. 2025). All prompts are identical to it, and its mle-solver and paper-solver are reused.
- The AI Scientist (Lu et al. 2024b) and Virtual Lab (Swanson et al. 2024).
- Self-consistency (Wang et al. 2023), self-agreement (Lin et al. 2023) and multi-chain reasoning (Yoran et al. 2023), as the nearest relatives of SDA.
- arXiv, bioRxiv and medRxiv, as the model for the preprint server. Retrieval uses SentenceTransformer cosine similarity.
- Ideas for fixes (the paper does not use these): ELO tournament evolution (Gottweis et al. 2025) and exploration rewards (Lehman and Stanley 2011; Schmidhuber 1991).
- Lange et al. 2025, cited for a reward-hacking memory exploit that humans overlooked.

CODE: none in the paper. The Appendix B.1 and B.2 tables hold the settings. The ones worth keeping are agent temperature 0.8, mle-solver steps 3, code repair attempts 2, paper-solver steps 1, and 40 papers per lab. The paper states that the hardware was a 2023 MacBook Pro (M3 Max, 36 GB).

FIGURES (read from the extracted text only; captions not run through the script)
- Fig 1, p.1: the overall framework of labs, humans and the shared server.
- Fig 3, p.7: the two-lab upload and retrieve flow. It is the clearest picture of the loop.
- Fig 4, p.8: the single-lab MATH-500 progression with callouts. Fig 5, p.9: panel A for benchmark transfer, panel B for the N=0 versus N=5 ablation, panel C for model transfer. Fig 6, p.11: the 3-lab parallel run against the sequential runs.
- Fig 5B is the one that carries the central claim, and Fig 6 shows the speed-up.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions in the PDF.
- The text extracted cleanly apart from broken kerning in a few table headings ("A ge n t L abor atory").
- The intro text cites Figure 1A and 1C, but the corresponding panels are described in Figures 4 and 5. The paper's own figure references are inconsistent. I did not view the figures.
